person: New parent in Nigeria, extended family household
situation: A new parent in a tropical household watches the cord stump stay wet for days and the mother-in-law pressures them to apply a binder ('put something like a binder on it') to help it dry.
trigger: Wet cord persisting past day 3; MIL observes and begins making indirect comments about 'doing something about it'.
context: Tropical climate (high humidity); extended family present in the home; MIL has authority in household decisions; no air conditioning; the cord is not drying as quickly as expected.
behaviour: Posted to r/newborns describing the MIL pressure
Identified the indirect communication pattern ('indirectly telling us')
Resisted the binder advice but felt unable to firmly refuse
constraint: Cultural deference to elder family members in the household; no clinical authority figure present to mediate.
thought: The cord is taking too long to dry. Maybe the MIL is right — maybe we should do something.
fear: The cord not falling off; the baby being uncomfortable; family conflict.
emotional_stake: Feeling incompetent as a new parent while being pressured by someone with more experience.
exact_language: My MIL wants to do something about it. I don't know what she wants to do but she is indirectly telling us to put something like a binder on it.
desired_change: A culturally respectful way to explain why the cord needs to dry naturally, without offending the MIL.

evidence_source.excerpt: My MIL wants to do something about it. I don't know what she wants to do but she is indirectly telling us to put something like a binder on it.
evidence_source.context: Parent in tropical climate describing MIL pressure to intervene; community advised leaving it alone.

observed_frequency: recurring across multiple forums and cultures
relationships: Same conflict pattern as CRF-PPL-CORD-CARE-004 but different household dynamics (both-parents + MIL vs FTM + MIL in American context)
